07_marg770: These are the words which Moses spoke, etc. The beginning of Deuteronomy seems to be the title of the whole work, because it indicates the person of the author, and what he did, and the place and the time. The name of the book too shows the grace of the New Testament. For Deuteronomy is interpreted "second law", and signifies the Gospel, which explains spiritually the sacraments of the Old Testament; as the book of Deuteronomy is a repetition of the four books of the law. For those contain their own matters in themselves; this one goes over them all again. It has its own sacraments too.
07_marg771: These are the words which Moses spoke, etc. He says this of himself as of another, after the manner of Holy Scripture; as there too: "Moses was the meekest of all men that dwelt upon earth." For so he avoids arrogance and shows that it is to be avoided. Likewise Job too says of himself: "There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job" etc. And John: "This is that disciple who giveth testimony of these things" etc.
07_marg772: He speaks of himself as of another, as John says of himself: "The disciple whom Jesus loved." Or the Holy Ghost bears witness to him, that no one might be able to doubt that Moses wrote these things.
07_marg773: It is asked why he said "these are the words which Moses spoke" and did not say "which God spoke"? And why he commands this book to be put in the ark and not the other books, in which are the words of the Lord? Again, how could he speak those words to all Israel, when so great a multitude was there to be cared for? Answer: he said this to show that he spoke to the people the same words which the Lord spoke to Moses. To the second it must be said that the books, in so far as they are the words of the Lord, need no commendation; but the book of Moses needed letters of commendation. For the Lord wishes the sayings of his own to be held in veneration, and not only his. And because this book is more expressive of the Gospel, therefore it is commanded to be put in the ark and held in greater reverence. To the third question: that Moses spoke to some and commanded them to speak to others; as it is said in Mark 9: "what I say to one, I say to all."

07_marg786: ISIDORE. Allegorically: in these kings, although the deed done is known, yet through the interpretations of the names a spiritual signification is intimated. For Sehon is interpreted "useless sprout" or "temptation of the eyes", by whom the devil is figured, who transforms himself into an angel of light, that by schisms or heresy he may deceive the unwary. Him the Amorrhites, that is, the embittering, have as king. For unless some pretence goes before, there will be neither heresies of the embittering nor schisms of the provoking. He is slain in each one when pretence is condemned and truth is loved. But Og is interpreted "shutting in", Basan "confusion". For the devil does this, that he may shut off the way to God, setting idolatry in the way, lest anyone believe in Christ. For shutting in goes before as king, confusion follows as people. For those whom he shuts out from the faith of Christ will be confounded when Christ appears. And Sehon dwelt in Hesebon, because the devil, the king of vices, mingles himself with human thoughts and girds the mind with superfluous cares, lest it utter words of truth or exercise works of godliness. For Hesebon is interpreted "thought" or "girdle of grief". Og too, king of Basan, dwelt in Astaroth and Edrai. For Astaroth [means] courts; Edrai, flood of evils; they sound unbelief, namely with wicked works. For the devil strives for this: that those whom he rules may never enter the door of faith, but, remaining outside, may always be busy with wicked works.

07_marg806: AND WHEN WE WERE COME INTO CADESBARNE, etc. That in the second year of its going out the people came into the desert of Pharan, which is Cades, where, the spies having returned with the fruits of the land and announcing what they had seen, they murmured against Moses and Aaron, and therefore, afflicted with the weariness of a long journey and with mortality, they perished: this place will give manifest judgment. Where it is to be noted that the forty-two mansions which they had from Egypt as far as the Jordan seem to fit only three courses of years, namely the first, the second, and the fortieth of the going out of Egypt. The first, by a certain distinction, contains twelve: the first, Ramesses, entered on the fifteenth day of the first month; the last, the wilderness of Sinai, reached on the first day of the third month, and not left for eleven continuous months for the sake of building the tabernacle and teaching the law. Of which twelve mansions only nine are expressed by name in Exodus; three are signified without distinction under the name of the desert of Sin (which is said to be between Elim and Sinai). The second year comprises twenty-one mansions; of which, all being comprehended without distinction in the order of the history under the name of the wilderness of Pharan, only the first and second and last, that is, the graves of lust, Haseroth, and Cades, are distinguished by name. But in the catalogue of mansions all alike are shown, how many they are in number, or by what name they are called. The first mansion, that is, the graves of lust, was entered in the second month of the same second year, on the twenty-second day of the month. For in the second year (as the scripture says), in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, they moved the camp from the desert of Sinai, and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Pharan. They set out from the mountain of the Lord a journey of three days, until they came to the place of the mansion which, by the merit of the people lusting for flesh, received the name of the graves of lust. On what day or month of the same year the last of these, that is, Cades, was entered is not said; yet that it lies in the wilderness of Pharan, because it was reached in the same year, is not passed over in silence. For it is written: The people did not move from that place until Mary was called back. And setting out from Haseroth, having pitched their tents in the desert of Pharan, where the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Send men to view the land of Chanaan. Which, lest it be thought commanded and done at the very next mansion after Haseroth, [it is shown] fulfilled in the last of those which are contained under the name of Pharan. Below it is written: "And the spies of the land, returning after forty days, having gone round the whole country", came to Moses in Pharan, which is Cades. In Deuteronomy too Moses says to the people: When you were come into Cadesbarne I said to you: You are come to the mountain of the Amorrhite, etc. And you said: "Let us send men who may view the land" etc. And that they reached the same mansion in the second year of their going out, from which yet, by the sin of murmuring, they deserved to turn back and wander long through the desert and fall here and there, Moses bears witness in what follows, saying: You abode in Cadesbarne a long time; and setting out thence we came into the wilderness that leadeth to the Red Sea, as the Lord had said to me; and we compassed mount Seir a long time. And below: The time that we walked from Cadesbarne to the torrent Zared was thirty-eight years, until the whole generation of the men of war was consumed. And Zared is not the name of any mansion of the forty-two, but of a torrent, to which (as is read in the book of Numbers), having passed the thirty-eighth mansion, named Ijeabarim, they came; leaving which, he says, they camped over against the Arnon, which is in the desert and juts out in the borders of the Amorrhite; which it is not hidden was done in the fortieth year. This last [year] contains ten mansions of the very long way through the desert; of which the first, regained with great labour, is the same, namely that Cades of the desert of Sin, which thirty-eight years before, their fault requiring it, they left behind them, turning back; of which it is written: "The children of Israel came into the desert of Sin in the first month, and the people abode in Cades; and Mary died there, and was buried in the same place. And when the people wanted water, they came together against Moses and Aaron" etc., as far as this: "This is the water of contradiction" etc. It is to be noted that the same Cades is set both in the desert of Pharan and in the desert of Sin, as the scripture relates; whence we conjecture that the part of the desert of Pharan where Cades is is specially called Sin. But this Sin is not that which they passed through as soon as they had crossed the Red Sea, between Elim and Sinai, but another altogether, and written among the Hebrews with other letters. The second mansion of the same fortieth year is mount Hor, on which Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month; the last, the plains of Moab upon the Jordan over against Jericho, where they abode meditating Deuteronomy until, Moses being dead, under Josue as leader they crossed the Jordan on the first day of the tenth month. The mansions of the first year, then, are twelve, of the second twenty-one; of the last ten, that twenty-first, which is Cades, being itself one, and nine others; together, in all, forty-two.
07_marg807: AND YOU CAME TO ME, etc. In the book of Numbers it is written that the Lord said to Moses that he should send men to view the land. But here the people is read to have said: Let us send men to view the land. But the people suggested this first to Moses; Moses referred the counsel to the Lord, according to whose command he afterwards sent the spies.
07_marg808: I SENT OF YOU TWELVE MEN, etc. ISIDORE. The twelve spies sent to spy out the fertile land, who terrified the people, bear the figure of the scribes and Pharisees. For as those were sent by Moses to view carefully the fertile land, so these by the law and the prophets, that through the searching of scripture they might watch for the coming of Christ, in whom was the land, that is, the holy flesh, in which they might obtain the kingdom of God and the fertility of spiritual fruits, and life eternal. But as those terrified the people with despair, lest they trust in God's promise, so the scribes and Pharisees persuaded the people not to believe in Christ, returning to the Egypt of this world, rejecting the manna of faith, seeking the black pots of sins and the rotten onions of blasphemers and the melons withering with the corruption of vices and lusts. And the cluster which two carried is Christ hanging on the wood of the cross, promised to the Gentiles, brought from the land of promise, from the womb of the virgin. The two bearers who go under the burden of the cluster are the two peoples. The former, the Jewish, blind and turned away, ignorant of the grace of him who hangs, and pressed by the burden of the one suspended, is put under it as he judges, according to that: "Let their eyes be darkened that they see not, and bow down their back always." But the latter, the Gentile, believing in Christ, having him always before his eyes, and following as a servant his Lord and a disciple his master, and hearing that saying of the Gospel: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me." This is the cluster which poured out the wine of its blood for our salvation in the crushing of the cross, and gave the Church to drink the pressed cup of its passion. This is the cluster which the pomegranates, that is, mother Church, followed; having a number of grains, that is, a multitude of peoples, and the redness of the blood of Christ glittering with its seal; it has also distinct grains, namely divers charisms. Judging themselves unworthy of all these, the unbelievers would not receive the land of the flesh of Christ flowing with milk and honey; which his servants, that is, the Christians, have obtained, of whose doctrine the Church sings: "How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth." And the fig signifies the law, as the cluster bears the figure of the Saviour; because neither is Christ without the law, nor the law without Christ.

07_marg816: ISIDORE. In Mary prophecy seems to have died; in Moses and Aaron, the law and priesthood of the Jews, who could not go up to the land of promise nor lead the believing people out of the wilderness of this world; but only Jesus, that is, the Saviour, the true Son of God. In the thirty-third mansion Moses offended the Lord. For, troubled by the murmuring of the people, doubting, he struck the rock, as though God could not give water from the rock, because he had not done so before. Moses in this place bears the figure of the people set under the law. For so the people fastened Christ to the wood of the cross, not believing him to be the power of God; as Moses, when he struck the rock, doubted of the power of God. But from the rock struck water flowed, and the wound of Christ was given back as life to believers. For the rock was Christ. This carnal despair about the divinity of Christ the Lord commands to die in the height of Christ himself, when he commands Moses to die on the mountain. For Christ is the rock, Christ the mountain: the rock, lowly strength; the mountain, towering greatness. Of this mountain it is said: A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid, etc. The prudence of the flesh lives when the humility of Christ on the cross is despised as a rock struck. The prudence of the flesh dies when Christ is acknowledged as exalted, as the eminence of a mountain.

07_marg817: AND WHEN READY ARMED, etc. This sentence strikes at human pride, which presumes on its own strength and does not trust in the power of God. For the Amorrhites, that is, the embittering, are the spiritual enemies who dwell on the mountains of pride and kill the presumptuous from Seir to Horma, that is, from the filth of vices to the damnation of punishments. For Seir is "hairy"; Horma is interpreted "anathema". For whoever does not fear to be polluted with the filth of vices must, according to his merits, be handed over to the fires of Gehenna. For the demons wish to entangle us in earthly desires; and if we persevere in sins and do not cease to go up the mountain of pride, they cut us down with fiery darts and lead us to perpetual anathema. Therefore let us not, after the manner of the Pelagians, presume on our own power, but, considering our infirmity, let us obey the Lord in all things, that, the enemies having been overcome, we may obtain the promised joys of the heavenly fatherland.

07_marg820: Seir is a mountain in the land of Edom, on which Esau dwelt, in the region of Gebalene, where the Horrhite dwelt before, whom Chodorlahomor slew; which received from Esau, hairy and shaggy, the name Seir, that is, "of the hairy one". 07_marg821: TO THE CHILDREN OF LOT I HAVE GIVEN AR IN POSSESSION, etc. Ar is the metropolis of the Moabites, upon the bank of the torrent Arnon, once possessed by a most ancient nation, the Emims; afterwards held by the children of Lot, that is, the Moabites, the inhabitants having been overthrown. It is shown today on the top of a mountain; but the torrent, coming down through steep places, flows into the Dead Sea. Allegorically. Ar is interpreted "he raised up"; Emims, that is, "the terrible". These are the demons, who raise up strifes and contentions and prepare the darts of wickedness against the faithful. The Enacims too, begotten of the stock of Enac and equalled to the giants in tallness, according to their name signify the demons. For [Enac] is interpreted "necklace on a lofty neck". For, lifted up with the haughtiness of pride, they ascribe all the equipment of their warfare to their own strength. Therefore they easily yield to those who trust in the strength of God and say with the Psalmist: "The Lord is my strength and my praise" etc.

07_marg822: FROM CADESBARNE, etc. JEROME. Cadesbarne is a place in the desert which is joined to the city of Petra in Arabia, where Mary died, and Moses, the rock having been struck, gave water to the thirsting people. The tomb of Mary is shown there even today; and the princes of Amalec too were slain there by Chodorlahomor.
07_marg823: SO I SENT MESSENGERS, etc. Allegorically. Sehon signifies the devil, for [the name] is "useless sprout" or "unfruitful tree" or "lifted up". Israel [signifies] the Christian people, which desires to pass through the way of this world and come to the heavenly kingdoms. This people sends to Sehon, promising with peaceable words that it will not dwell in his land, but only pass through and go by the king's way. This each one promised when he first came to the water of baptism and received the first seals of the faith. For he renounced the devil and his pomps and works and all his service and pleasures. This is what is said: "that Israel will not turn aside into his field or into his vineyard, and will not drink water from his cistern"; that is, will no longer take up the discipline either of astrology or of magic or of any doctrine that is against godliness. His people are the princes and judges of the world and all the ministers of wickedness, who persecute the people of God. But the faith which they hold in outward show rebukes them, lest they grow numb with idleness, lest by their example they draw others away from labour and longsuffering. Whence it is said to them through Moses: "Shall your brethren go to fight, and will you sit here? Why do ye overturn the minds of the children of Israel?" 07_marg834: AUGUSTINE. Perhaps by these two words he signified one thing. Or he called a likeness a statue, or an image not expressed by imitating the features of any man. For that a thing made by such expression is called an image no one would doubt; so that every image is a likeness, but not conversely. For in twins who are alike, there is the likeness of each in the other, not an image. But if a son is like his father, he is rightly called an image, so that the father is the prototype, that is, the first figure, from which that image is seen to be expressed. Of these images some are of the same substance, as a son; others not, as a picture. Whence that which is written: "God made man to his own image" is to be so understood that the image which was made is not of the same substance. For if it were of the same, it would be said not made but begotten. And that he did not add "and likeness", as above, seems to have been done because where there is an image, [there is also] a likeness. Whence here too Moses forbids a likeness and an image to be made. But in the Decalogue it is said that no likeness is to be made, nor is an image mentioned. For if there is no likeness, there is no image; since if there is an image, there is a likeness. Lastly, where he forbade a likeness and an image, he wished men to be understood, where a likeness can be made, not properly of this or that man, but of anyone; and an image, that is, properly of this or that man. But when he spoke of irrational animals, he said only "likeness". For no one sets up for himself one dog or the like, looking at which he paints or fashions an image, as is customary with men.

The seventh: Thou shalt not steal; in which he forbids all robbery. The eighth: Thou shalt not bear false witness; he abhors the crime of lying and falsehood. 07_marg848: THOU SHALT LOVE THE LORD THY GOD, etc. AUGUSTINE. Charity will not be taken away, but fulfilled. When it has contemplated what it believed and obtained what it hoped, in that fulness this precept will be fulfilled. For while there is in us anything of carnal concupiscence which is bridled even by restraint, God will not be loved altogether with the whole soul. For the flesh does not lust without the soul, although the flesh is said to lust, because the soul lusts carnally. But then there will be no law in the members fighting against the law of the mind, but God will be loved by the soul with the whole heart, the whole mind. And this perfection ought to have been commanded to man, although in this life it cannot be had. For one does not run rightly if he does not know how he is to run. And we run by hoping, believing and desiring, by giving alms and praying, that running we may be helped; and so let us hear the precepts of perfection, and not neglect to run toward the fulness of charity. Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, etc., and thy neighbour as thyself. On these the whole law hangs and the prophets. The end of the precept, then, is the twofold love, namely of God and of the neighbour; and if you understand yourself whole, that is, soul and body, and your neighbour likewise whole (for man consists of soul and body), no kind of things to be loved has been passed over in these two. For since the love of God runs before, its measure is prescribed, that all other things should flow together into him. Of love of yourself nothing seems to be said; but where it is said "as thyself", that you should love yourself is not passed over. And he loves in order who does not love what is not to be loved and loves what is to be loved; and does not love more what is less to be loved, nor equally what is to be loved more or less, nor more or less what is equally to be loved. Every sinner, in so far as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; but every man, in so far as he is a man, is to be loved for God's sake; but God for his own sake. And if God is to be loved more than every man, each one ought to love him more than himself. Likewise another man is to be loved more than our body; because all these things are to be loved for God's sake, and another man can enjoy God with us, which the body cannot, because it lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God. And all are to be loved equally; but since you cannot do good to all, you must take thought chiefly for those who, by the occasion of places and times or of anything else, are more closely joined to us.
07_marg849: THOU SHALT LOVE THY GOD WITH THY WHOLE, etc. Through the love of God the love of neighbour is begotten, and through the love of neighbour the love of God is nourished. For he who neglects to love God does not know how to love his neighbour. And we are more fully perfected in the love of God if in the bosom of his love we rejoice in charity toward our neighbour. About to say, then, "thou shalt love thy neighbour", he set first "thou shalt love the Lord thy God"; that first he may fix in us the root of his love, and afterwards brotherly love may spread its branches. And that the love of God grows together with the love of neighbour, John shows, saying: "He that loveth not his brother whom he seeth, how can he love God whom he seeth not?" The love of God is born through fear, but in growing it is changed into affection. And that it may be shown how far each is from the charity of neighbour or how far he has advanced in it, God presses some down with scourges, props up others with successes. For often those pursue us when we are wretched who venerate us beyond comparison when we are happy. But when one loves or is loved in prosperity, it is uncertain whether the prosperity or the person is loved. For in good times a friend is not known, and in evil times an enemy is not hidden.

07_marg854: ISIDORE. The seven nations are the seven principal vices, which the spiritual soldier, overcoming them through the grace of God, is commanded to exterminate. They are said to be of greater number because the vices are more than the virtues. In the catalogue they are called seven nations; in the conquest they are set down without number: but when he shall have destroyed many nations before thee. For the people of carnal things, which is multiplied from the sevenfold tinder of the vices, is more numerous than Israel. From gluttony: revelling, drunkenness. From fornication: filthy speech, scurrility, jesting and foolish talk. From avarice: lying, fraud, thefts, perjuries, desire of filthy lucre, false witness, violence, inhumanity and rapacity. From anger: murder, clamour and indignation. From sadness: rancour, faintheartedness, bitterness, despair and sloth. From acedia: idleness, drowsiness, importunity, restlessness of mind and body, instability, wordiness and curiosity. From vainglory: contentions, heresies, boasting and presumption of novelties. From pride: contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction and many others. These, though they are of greater number than the virtues, yet when the principal ones are overcome all are quieted and are destroyed by a perpetual death. And that these plagues are stronger we feel in temptation; for the delight of carnal passions fights more strongly in our members than the pursuits of the virtues, which are acquired with the utmost contrition of heart and body. We possess the regions of these nations with the army of Israel, that is, we overcome the vices with the virtues, so that in our heart chastity may hold the place of fornication, patience the place of fury, saving joy the place of sadness, fortitude dwell in the place of acedia, humility in the place of pride; so, each vice being driven out, in their place may reign the sons of Israel, that is, souls seeing God. 07_marg873: AUGUSTINE. In Exodus Moses is related to have written the ten words of the law on the tables; in Deuteronomy, God himself. In Exodus also [it is said] that the former tables were written with the finger of God, but the second were kept in the ark and in the tabernacle. We have said that they signify the two testaments: so that in the Old Testament the law might be commended as the work of God, where man did nothing, because the law cannot be fulfilled [by man]; for the work of the law is truly done by charity, not by fear, which is the grace of the New Testament. But on the second tables man is read to have written the words of God, because man can do the work of the law through the charity of justice, which he cannot do through the fear of punishment. When therefore it is read in Deuteronomy: "And he wrote", etc., namely "in the tables, according as he had written before", etc., God is read to have written both tables, and not man. In Exodus [too] the Lord says: "I will write on the tables the words that were in the former", etc. Exodus alone, then, raises the question; for a little after it is said: "Write thee these words", etc., and after a few [words] it adds: "and he wrote upon the tables the words of the covenant." For if it be understood thus: "Write thee these words", namely other words, which are not written on the tables but in the book of the law, certainly what follows: "And he was there with the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread, and he wrote upon the tables the ten words of the covenant", shows that Moses wrote on the tables, not God; unless by force we understand "the Lord" and not Moses, and so there will be no difference of the testaments, since God wrote both the former and the second tables. Yet the former, without doubt, God, not man, both made and wrote; for it was not then said to Moses: "Hew thee two tables", but thus it is read: "Moses came down from the mount, and the two tables in his hands; and the tables were the work of God, and the writing [of God]." Above too it had been said: "He gave Moses tables of stone written with the finger of God." But Moses is commanded to hew the second, that they may be understood to be hewn by human work, although God wrote [them]. And both are said of the second tables for this reason: that God by his grace does the work of the law in man, and man, receiving the grace of God through faith (which belongs to the New Testament), is a fellow worker with God who helps him. Therefore in the first only the work of God is mentioned, because the law is spiritual and holy, and the commandment holy, where there is no work of man, because the unbelievers do not submit themselves to the help of God's grace, but wish to establish their own justice, and the law is to them for damnation; which the breaking of the tables signifies. And for this reason above God promised that he would write, and in Deuteronomy he is related not only to have promised but also to have written. For God works in us both to will and to accomplish and to perfect, and we work out our salvation with fear and trembling; and he helps the choice of the good will.

07_marg931: WHEN [THY BROTHER] IS SOLD TO THEE, etc. ISIDORE. If a Hebrew boy has come into servitude, it is commanded that he serve six years and be freed in the seventh. If he will not, because of his wife and children, his ear will be bored and he will be a servant for ever. This is not said of the present world but of the future: because, serving in the six ages of this world, on the seventh day, that is, in the eternal sabbath, we are freed, if only we have willed to be free while in the world we serve sin. But if we will not, our ear will be bored in testimony of disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we preferred to being freed, that is, with the flesh and its works, namely sins, we shall serve for ever.
07_marg932: WHEN [THY BROTHER] IS SOLD TO THEE, etc. A Hebrew is a passer-over, one who strives, namely, toward the eternal fatherland and passes from vices to virtues, from earthly things to heavenly. If such a one sells himself to thee, that is, binds himself to thy teaching, thou shalt teach him to strive to work in the present life so that he may come to rest. This is: he shall serve thee six years. In the seventh year thou shalt let him go free, nor suffer him to go away empty; as promising him eternal rewards and true freedom in the other life. But if he say: "I will not go out", because he loves thee and thy house, that is, if he has done the good things he did not for eternal reward but for human praise, as one loving the present life, thou shalt bore his ear with an awl, that is, thou shalt prick his mind with the terror of judgment, at the door of the house; because the judgment will be at the going out of this life and the going in of the other; and he shall serve thee for ever, that is, thou shalt teach him that if he has loved the world more than God he is to be delivered over to eternal punishments.
07_marg933: Though the active life and the contemplative are [given] us by the grace of God, the one is of necessity, the other of will. For no one who knows God enters the kingdom without the active life, but many do without the contemplative. "If thou buy a Hebrew servant", etc. A Hebrew, that is, one passing over, is bought when each one who passes over in mind from the world is subjected to the service of God. He is commanded to serve six years, that in the seventh he may be freed for nothing. In six the perfection of the active life is expressed, in seven the contemplative. He serves six years and goes out free in the seventh, because through the active life perfectly carried through he passes to the freedom of the contemplative life. For nothing: because when we have done well we are unprofitable servants. As therefore the active life is of gift, so also is the contemplative. With what raiment he came in, with such let him go out: because it is necessary that each one persevere in what he has begun. For he passes well to the contemplative life who in the active has not changed the course of his intention. But some love to work well before they are joined to the service of God, others after they have come to his service. He then who had good working before was bought with a wife. He can pass to the contemplative life and yet not forsake the active; whence the wife goes out with him. For passing to contemplation he does not leave the affection of good work by which he may profit others. "The woman and her children shall be her master's." When the servant is bought, the master gives him a wife, when the preacher joins to good action him whom he has delivered to the Lord. For preachers are called masters; whence: "Dost thou know that the Lord will take away thy master from thee?" The wife bears sons and daughters when good action begets strong or tender fruits. This woman with her children remains to the master; the servant goes out with his raiment: because good action and its fruits are credited to the preacher, while he himself, with the intention of desire, goes out free to contemplation through grace. If the servant say [I love my master]: he loves his master when he guards the preacher's words with careful mind; he loves his wife and children, namely the active life and its fruits. The master brings him to the gods and sets him to the door and the posts, and bores his ear with an awl, that he may be a servant for ever: because the preacher imbues him with the sayings of the ancient fathers, at the door and posts of the tabernacle, that he may hear of the entry into the eternal tabernacle and acknowledge the terror of judgment, lest he seek glory from men for his good works. The ear is bored with an awl when his mind is pierced by the subtlety of the fear of God, so that, transfixed by the point of the word, it may ever attend to the entry of the kingdom, as though bored at the door and post of the tabernacle. He will be a servant in the world, that he may be free after the world. For now not only is the active life in servitude, but even contemplation does not obtain freedom of mind, because it sees the inmost rest in a dark manner.

07_marg935: He shows the difference among the Greeks between "firstlings" and "first-borne"; he shows also that where among the Latins Christ is called firstborn, among the Greeks he is called prototokos.
07_marg936: OF THE FIRSTLINGS. Those are called firstborn which first open the womb and come forth at the first birth. But in Greek "prototoka" are those which belong to the first bearing of the female, as it were "first-borne" [protoparta], not "protogena", that is, first-begotten. Whence Christ is not called "monotokos" of the Father, but "monogenes", that is, only-begotten, namely the only one. But where in Latin he is called the firstborn from the dead, in Greek he is called "prototokos", not "protogenes", as though the Father had both begotten one equal to himself and brought forth a creature. For in that he is called the firstborn of every creature, that is, "prototokos", it can be understood according to the new creature, of which it is said: "If then any be in Christ a new creature"; of which he is the first, because he first so rose that he dies no more, which is promised at the end to the new creature which is in him. Yet it raises a difficulty that in Proverbs it is said: "Firstborn, I say to thee, son." For if the father speaks to the son, he calls the same one firstborn whom [he calls] only-begotten: [firstborn,] because we too are sons of God; but he is only-begotten because he alone is of the substance of the Father, equal and coeternal.
07_marg937: Not to thyself, but to the giver of all, because every best gift is from above. But what is light in our thought, or spotted in our conversation, or lame in the progress of works, or blind through ignorance of mind, or deformed or feeble in any part, we ought not to sacrifice to God, that is, impute to him, but to ourselves.
07_marg938: GREGORY. To plough with the firstling of a bullock is to publish the beginnings of good conversation in the exercise of action. To shear the firstlings of the sheep is to strip the good things that are beginning of the hidden covering of reason. For if we begin to practise anything good and strong, we ought not quickly to show it. And what is simple and harmless ought not to be stripped of its veil. [Let them be kept] for the divine sacrifices alone, [lest,] mingled with carnal life, they become known too soon, and the mind, deceived when its good things are praised, fail to detect the evils that are in them.

07_marg939: BUT IF IT HAVE, etc. There are some works which, though they please God less, yet profit the neighbour; and if they cannot be offered to God, they can be eaten. For though they please God less, because the intention (which God looks on) is darkened, yet they help neighbours by example, like the roe and the hart. The roe goes by leaps; the hart is an enemy to the serpent, and leaping over rough and thorny places it climbs the mountains. And therefore they are taken in a good sense.
